title: Thunder at Spurs, October 20: Three Things to Watch on Opening Night
description: A beginner-friendly guide to Oklahoma City at San Antonio: the start time, playoff context, and three possession battles to follow.

sections.heading: When and where
paragraphs: Oklahoma City visits San Antonio at Frost Bank Center on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. Tip-off is scheduled for 8:30 p.m. in San Antonio, 9:30 p.m. Eastern, or 01:30 UTC on October 21. It is an opening-night regular-season game. The NBA's published U.S. broadcast schedule lists NBC and Peacock; availability elsewhere depends on your country.

sections.heading: Why this matchup has a story already
paragraphs: The Spurs eliminated the Thunder in a seven-game Western Conference finals series in 2026. Opening night offers a fresh look at that matchup, with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Victor Wembanyama among the central players to follow if available. The previous series is useful background, but it does not decide what happens in this game. Here are three questions that make the action easier to read.

sections.heading: 1. Where does the first good shot come from?
paragraphs: When Gilgeous-Alexander handles the ball, watch the defenders around him as well as the dribble. Does one defender stay in front, or does another move across to help? If help arrives, follow the next pass and see whether it creates space for a teammate. At the other end, track where Wembanyama receives the ball and how the defense responds. These are things to observe, not a promise that either team will use one fixed tactic.

sections.heading: 2. Who ends the possession after a miss?
paragraphs: Do not stop watching when a shot hits the rim. The rebound determines whether the attacking team gets another opportunity or the defense can move the other way. Look for the player who makes room for a teammate to collect the ball, not only the player credited with the rebound. A missed shot followed by an offensive rebound is a different outcome from a miss that immediately sends the opponent into attack.

sections.heading: 3. What happens in the first seconds of the next attack?
paragraphs: After a rebound or turnover, look up the floor. Is there an immediate pass forward, a dribble into open space, or a pause while everyone takes their positions? This simple check helps distinguish transition opportunities from attacks against a defense that is already set. If one team strings together several scores, rewind to how those possessions began instead of assuming every basket came from the same problem.

sections.heading: Use one possession as your viewing unit
paragraphs: Try the three-question checklist for a short stretch: how was the shot created, who collected the miss, and how did the next attack start? You can enjoy the star matchup while noticing the teammates who connect those moments. Starting lineups and player availability still need a check close to tip-off; this guide does not treat either as confirmed.
